DERMATOLOGICAL__Rash:
“Rash” is not a diagnosis — it is a starting point. The first question is never “what is it called?” but “is the patient sick, and are there red flags?”
  • Fever with a non-blanching rash is meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise → antibiotics now (see meningococcal disease, petechiae & purpura).
  • A painful rash with mucosal erosions and blistering is Stevens-Johnson / toxic epidermal necrolysis — stop the drug (see dermatological emergencies); urticaria with airway or breathing compromise is anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline (see anaphylaxis); and >90% erythema is erythroderma (see erythroderma).
  • Only once these are cleared do you describe the morphology (macular / papular, purpuric, vesicular / bullous, pustular, wheals, scaly plaques), the distribution and the time course, and route to the specific pattern — eczema, psoriasis, urticaria, a drug or viral exanthem (see eczema, psoriasis).
  • SCAM: Site, Configuration, Arrangement, Morphology.
🚨Some rashes are emergencies. Look for the warning signs: a non-blanching purpuric rash with fever (meningococcal sepsis → benzylpenicillin now) (see meningococcal disease); skin pain / tenderness, mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals), blistering, skin detachment and a positive Nikolsky sign (SJS / TEN, or DRESS with fever, facial oedema and eosinophilia) — stop the culprit drug (see dermatological emergencies, blistering rash); urticaria with lip / tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor or hypotension (anaphylaxis) (see anaphylaxis); widespread erythema >90% with systemic upset (erythroderma); and rapidly spreading erythema with pain out of proportion (necrotising fasciitis) or monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczema (eczema herpeticum) (see skin infections).

1Confirm & classify
🚩Meningococcal sepsis
  • Fever + a non-blanching purpuric / petechial rash + systemically unwell
  • → immediate antibiotics (benzylpenicillin / ceftriaxone) + resuscitation, do not wait (see meningococcal disease, petechiae & purpura)
  • Glass (tumbler) test; may have meningism, shock
🚩SJS / TEN & drug emergencies
  • Painful rash + mucosal erosions (mouth, eyes, genitals) + blisters + skin detachment (Nikolsky+)
  • A drug trigger 1–3 weeks before — stop the culprit, dermatological emergency (see dermatological emergencies, blistering rash)
  • DRESS: fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, organ involvement
🚩Anaphylaxis / angioedema
  • Urticaria + lip / tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor, hypotension
  • → IM adrenaline, ABC, remove trigger (see anaphylaxis, urticaria)
  • Rapid onset after food / drug / sting
🟠Erythroderma
  • >90% of the skin red and scaly + systemic upset
  • Fluid / heat / protein loss, high-output failure, sepsis risk (see erythroderma)
  • Causes: eczema, psoriasis, drugs, lymphoma (Sézary)
🟠Serious skin infection
  • Cellulitis (hot, spreading, tender erythema + fever) (see cellulitis)
  • Necrotising fasciitis (pain out of proportion, crepitus, rapid) — surgical emergency
  • Eczema herpeticum (monomorphic punched-out erosions), staph scalded skin (see skin infections)
🩹Common inflammatory dermatoses
  • Eczema (itchy, flexural), psoriasis (scaly extensor plaques) (see eczema, psoriasis)
  • Urticaria (transient wheals), contact dermatitis (see contact dermatitis)
  • Viral exanthem, pityriasis rosea, lichen planus
Sick or not sick, first. Before naming a rash, screen for the emergencies: non-blanching + fever, mucosae + blisters + skin pain, urticaria + airway, >90% erythema. Everything else is described by morphology, distribution and time course.

DERMATOLOGICAL__Pruritus:
Pruritus is the sensation that provokes scratching. The single most useful division is: is there a primary rash, or not?
  • An itch with a rash is usually a skin disease — eczema, scabies, urticaria, lichen planus, dermatitis herpetiformis, bullous pemphigoid (see eczema, scabies, urticaria).
  • An itch without a rash (skin normal apart from excoriations) points to a systemic cause: cholestasis (obstructive jaundice, primary biliary cholangitis) (see jaundice, primary biliary cholangitis), chronic kidney disease (uraemic) (see chronic kidney disease), iron deficiency and thyroid disease, haematological disease (polycythaemia — itch after a hot bath; Hodgkin lymphoma) (see polycythaemia, plethora, lymphoma), malignancy (paraneoplastic), drugs (opioids), HIV and pregnancy.
  • Always look for the red-flag trio: lymphadenopathy, jaundice and weight loss.
🚨Persistent itch without a rash can be the first sign of serious disease. Think Hodgkin lymphoma (itch with night sweats, weight loss and rubbery lymphadenopathy) and other paraneoplastic itch (see lymphoma). Cholestatic itch with painless jaundice, pale stools and weight loss may be pancreatic or biliary cancer (see pancreatic cancer, jaundice). In pregnancy, itch of the palms and soles without a rash in the third trimester is intrahepatic cholestasis of pregnancy — a fetal risk needing bile acids and monitoring (see medical disorders in pregnancy). And aquagenic pruritus (itch after a warm bath) suggests polycythaemia vera (see polycythaemia).

  • Chronic kidney disease (uraemic itch) (see chronic kidney disease)

  • Eczema (itchy, flexural), urticaria (wheals) (see eczema, urticaria)

DERMATOLOGICAL__Purpuric Rash:
A purpuric rash is non-blanching — blood has leaked into the skin (confirm with the glass test). The dermatological question that organises the causes is morphology: is it non-palpable, palpable, or retiform / necrotic?
  • Non-palpable (macular) purpura is a platelet or vessel problem — thrombocytopenia, anticoagulants, or fragile vessels (senile, steroid, scurvy) (see thrombocytopenia).
  • Palpable purpura means inflammation of the vessel wall — a small-vessel (leukocytoclastic) vasculitis (Henoch-Schönlein, drug, infection, ANCA-associated) (see vasculitis, paediatric vasculitis).
  • Retiform / necrotic (net-like, angulated, black) purpura signals vessel occlusion — DIC, warfarin necrosis, antiphospholipid, calciphylaxis, cholesterol emboli (see DIC).
  • Over all of this sits the reflex rule: fever + purpura + unwell = meningococcal sepsis → antibiotics now (see meningococcal disease). For the full haematological and systemic work-up of purpura, see the petechiae & purpura note.
🚨Read the shape of the purpura. Fever with a spreading non-blanching rash in an unwell patient is meningococcal sepsis → immediate antibiotics, do not wait (see meningococcal disease). Retiform (net-like) or necrotic purpura is occlusive — think DIC / purpura fulminans (see DIC), warfarin skin necrosis (days after starting) (see anticoagulation), antiphospholipid syndrome, calciphylaxis and cholesterol emboli. Palpable purpura with renal, lung or gut involvement is a systemic vasculitis needing a biopsy and ANCA (see vasculitis). And splinter haemorrhages with fever and a new murmur point to infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Urticaria:
Urticaria is transient, itchy, raised wheals — each individual lesion lasts <24 hours, blanches, and migrates. It may come with angioedema (deeper, non-itchy swelling of the lips, tongue, eyelids or genitals).
  • First, is this anaphylaxis? — wheals with airway, breathing or circulatory compromise mean IM adrenaline now (see anaphylaxis).
  • Second, acute (<6 weeks) or chronic (>6 weeks)? Acute is usually allergic (food, drug, sting — IgE) or post-viral (see urticaria / angioedema). Chronic is spontaneous (autoimmune / idiopathic) or inducible (physical: dermographism, cold, cholinergic, pressure, solar).
  • Two traps: angioedema without weals (ACE-inhibitor or hereditary C1-esterase deficiency — antihistamine-resistant, laryngeal risk) (see drug reactions); and weals that last >24 hours, hurt and bruise — that is urticarial vasculitis (see vasculitis).
🚨Urticaria plus airway or breathing compromise is anaphylaxis. Wheals with lip / tongue swelling, wheeze, stridor or hypotension after a food, drug or sting → IM adrenaline, ABC and remove the trigger (see anaphylaxis). Angioedema without weals is a distinct danger: an ACE inhibitor or hereditary angioedema (C1-esterase-inhibitor deficiency) can cause laryngeal oedema that does not respond to antihistamines / adrenaline in the usual way (see drug reactions). And individual weals lasting >24 hours that are painful / burning and leave bruising or pigmentation are urticarial vasculitis — biopsy and look for connective tissue disease (see vasculitis, connective tissue disease).

  • Individual weals lasting >24 hours, painful / burning, leaving bruising / pigmentation

  • <6 weeks; IgE-mediated to food, drug (penicillin, NSAID), sting, latex

  • Daily / almost-daily weals for >6 weeks, no external trigger
  • Autoimmune / idiopathic; associated thyroid autoimmunity

DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythroderma:
Erythroderma is redness and scaling affecting >90% of the skin surface — a dermatological emergency in its own right, whatever the cause. The failing skin can no longer regulate temperature or hold fluid: expect hypothermia (or hyperthermia), dehydration, high-output cardiac failure, hypoalbuminaemia and secondary sepsis — so the first job is resuscitate and admit (see dermatological emergencies). Then find the cause. The classic five are eczema, psoriasis, drugs, cutaneous T-cell lymphoma (Sézary syndrome) and idiopathic (see eczema, psoriasis, lymphoma). Clues to the cause: a pre-existing dermatosis, a recent drug (with fever and eosinophilia = DRESS), lymphadenopathy with circulating Sézary cells, or islands of sparing (pityriasis rubra pilaris). The itch can be intense (see pruritus).
🚨Erythroderma kills through its complications. Widespread vasodilation and barrier loss cause fluid and electrolyte loss, temperature dysregulation (hypothermia), high-output cardiac failure, protein loss (hypoalbuminaemia, oedema) and secondary infection / sepsis — monitor obs, fluids, temperature and skin swabs, and admit (see dermatological emergencies). Look hard for two causes you must not miss: cutaneous T-cell lymphoma / Sézary syndrome (erythroderma + lymphadenopathy + circulating Sézary cells) (see lymphoma) and a drug reaction / DRESS (recent drug, fever, facial oedema, eosinophilia, deranged LFTs) — stop the culprit drug (see drug reactions).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Blistering Rash:
A blistering rash is a fluid-filled eruption — vesicles (<5 mm) or bullae (>5 mm). As always, screen for the emergency first: a painful rash with mucosal erosions and skin detachment is Stevens-Johnson / toxic epidermal necrolysis (see dermatological emergencies); monomorphic punched-out erosions on eczema with systemic upset is eczema herpeticum (see skin infections). Then sort by mechanism. Infective: herpes simplex / zoster (dermatomal), chickenpox, bullous impetigo, staph scalded skin (see viral infections). Immunobullous: bullous pemphigoid (tense, itchy, elderly) and pemphigus vulgaris (flaccid, mucosal, Nikolsky+) (see immunobullous disorders), and dermatitis herpetiformis (itchy, extensor, coeliac) (see coeliac disease). Reaction / physical / metabolic: fixed drug eruption, erythema multiforme, burns / friction, contact dermatitis, porphyria and diabetic bullae. Tense vs flaccid and Nikolsky are the key bedside splits.
🚨Some blisters are emergencies. Skin pain, mucosal involvement (mouth, eyes, genitals), sheets of detachment and a positive Nikolsky sign after a drug = SJS / TEN — stop the drug, treat like a burn (see dermatological emergencies). Monomorphic punched-out vesicles / erosions on eczema with fever = eczema herpeticum (disseminated HSV) → aciclovir; and staphylococcal scalded skin syndrome and bullous / necrotising infection spread fast (see skin infections, cellulitis). Pemphigus vulgaris (flaccid bullae + mucosal erosions) can be life-threatening from fluid loss and sepsis (see immunobullous disorders).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Alopecia:
The one question that decides everything in alopecia is: scarring or non-scarring? Part the hair and look at the scalp. If the follicular openings are lost and the scalp is smooth, shiny or inflamed, this is scarring (cicatricial) alopecia — the hair loss is permanent and needs an urgent scalp biopsy (lichen planopilaris, discoid lupus, folliculitis decalvans, frontal fibrosing alopecia) (see hair disorders, connective tissue disease). If the follicular openings are preserved, it is non-scarring and potentially reversible. Non-scarring splits into patchy — alopecia areata (smooth patches, exclamation-mark hairs, nail pitting), tinea capitis (scaly, broken hairs, children) (see skin infections), trichotillomania — and diffuse — telogen effluvium (after stress / illness / childbirth), androgenetic (pattern), and systemic causes (thyroid, iron deficiency, drugs, SLE) (see thyroid disease, anaemia).
🚨Scarring alopecia is a time-critical diagnosis. Loss of the follicular openings means the follicle is being destroyed — hair lost is lost for good, so a prompt scalp biopsy and treatment can save the surrounding hair (see hair disorders). Look for a systemic driver: discoid / systemic lupus (scarring plaques, photosensitive facial rash) (see connective tissue disease, rash). In children, tinea capitis with a boggy, pustular kerion can itself scar — treat with oral antifungals (see skin infections). And diffuse hair loss is a cue to check thyroid function and ferritin (see thyroid disease, anaemia).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Nail Changes:
The nails are a window on the whole patient. Read them systematically — shape, colour, surface, the nail fold and the free edge. The one change you must never dismiss is a single-digit longitudinal pigmented band that widens or spreads onto the nail fold (Hutchinson’s sign) — that is a subungual melanoma until biopsy says otherwise (see skin cancer). Beyond that, nail signs map to systemic disease: clubbing (lung / heart / GI disease) (see lung cancer), splinter haemorrhages (endocarditis, vasculitis) (see infective endocarditis), nailfold telangiectasia (connective tissue disease) (see connective tissue disease), pitting and onycholysis (psoriasis) (see psoriasis), koilonychia (iron deficiency) (see koilonychia) and leukonychia (liver disease / low albumin) (see leukonychia). Fungal nails, paronychia and trauma make up the local causes.
🚨One nail sign is a cancer until proven otherwise. A longitudinal pigmented band in a single nail that is widening, irregular, or spreads pigment onto the surrounding nail fold (Hutchinson’s sign) — especially a new band in an adult or one with nail dystrophy — is a subungual melanoma; refer urgently for dermoscopy and biopsy (see skin cancer). Splinter haemorrhages with fever and a new murmur point to infective endocarditis (see infective endocarditis). Clubbing is never normal — look for lung cancer, fibrosis, cyanotic heart disease, IBD or cirrhosis (see lung cancer). And nailfold changes with Raynaud’s flag a connective tissue disease (see connective tissue disease).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Pigmented Lesion:
Every pigmented lesion asks one question: could this be a melanoma? Screen with the ABCDE rule — Asymmetry, irregular Border, more than one Colour, Diameter >6 mm, and (most important) Evolving / changing — and the ugly-duckling sign (a mole that stands out from the patient’s others). A lesion that is new, changing, bleeding, itching or regressing earns an urgent (2-week-wait) referral (see skin cancer). Most pigmented lesions are benign: melanocytic naevi (symmetrical, stable, uniform) (see lesion morphology), seborrhoeic keratoses (stuck-on, warty, greasy) (see seborrhoeic keratosis), solar lentigines, dermatofibromas (see benign skin lumps) and freckles. Watch the special sites — face (lentigo maligna), palms / soles (acral) and under a nail (subungual) (see nail changes).
🚨A changing pigmented lesion is a melanoma until proven otherwise. Refer urgently a lesion that is ABCDE-positive, an ugly duckling, or new / changing / bleeding / ulcerating / itching / regressing in an adult (see skin cancer). Beware the deceptive forms: nodular melanoma (a rapidly growing, firm, elevated nodule — EFG: Elevated, Firm, Growing) which may be amelanotic; lentigo maligna (a slowly enlarging pigmented facial patch in the elderly); acral melanoma (palm / sole); and subungual melanoma (a single-nail pigmented band with Hutchinson’s sign) (see nail changes). Do not shave-biopsy a suspected melanoma — excise it so the Breslow thickness can be measured.

DERMATOLOGICAL__Leg Ulcers:
Most leg ulcers are vascular — venous (~70%, gaiter area, haemosiderin, varicose veins), arterial (punched-out, painful, absent pulses) or neuropathic (painless, over pressure points, in diabetes) — and that triad, with its ABPI-led work-up, is covered in the leg ulcers (vascular) note. This note is about the ulcer that is not simply venous, arterial or neuropathic — the atypical ulcer. Suspect it when an ulcer is in an unusual site, has an atypical edge, is disproportionately painful, is rapidly growing, or fails to heal despite correct treatment. The key atypical causes are malignancy (a rolled / everted edge, or a Marjolin’s ulcer in a chronic scar) (see skin cancer), pyoderma gangrenosum (a violaceous, undermined, rapidly enlarging painful ulcer) (see pyoderma gangrenosum), vasculitis (punched-out ulcers on livedo / purpura) (see vasculitis, livedo reticularis) and infection (see cellulitis).
🚨Biopsy the ulcer that will not heal. A leg ulcer with a rolled or everted edge, that is enlarging, or that arises in a chronic scar / long-standing ulcer may be a squamous cell carcinoma (Marjolin’s ulcer) or BCC — take an edge biopsy (see skin cancer). Pyoderma gangrenosum (a rapidly enlarging, exquisitely painful ulcer with a violaceous, undermined border and pathergy) is worsened by debridement — it needs immunosuppression, and a hunt for IBD or rheumatoid arthritis (see pyoderma gangrenosum, IBD). And painful, punched-out ulcers on a background of livedo or palpable purpura with systemic symptoms are a vasculitis (see vasculitis).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Photosensitive Rash:
A photosensitive rash follows the light. It sits on sun-exposed sites — the face, the V of the neck, the dorsal hands and extensor forearms — and characteristically spares the shaded areas: under the chin, behind the ears, the upper eyelids, and skin under clothing. Recognising that photodistribution is the whole diagnosis. The causes divide into: drug-induced (phototoxic / photoallergic — doxycycline, thiazides, amiodarone, NSAIDs, quinolones) (see drug reactions); connective tissue disease — lupus (malar / discoid) and dermatomyositis (heliotrope, Gottron’s) (see connective tissue disease, malar rash); polymorphic light eruption (itchy papules hours after sun, young women, spring); porphyria (skin fragility / blisters, or burning) (see cutaneous signs of systemic disease); and photoaggravated dermatoses (rosacea, eczema) (see rosacea, eczema).
🚨A photosensitive rash can be the skin sign of systemic autoimmune disease. A photosensitive malar or discoid rash with arthralgia, mouth ulcers, serositis or renal disease is lupus — check ANA / anti-Ro / dsDNA (see connective tissue disease, malar rash). Dermatomyositis — a heliotrope (violaceous eyelid) rash, Gottron’s papules, the shawl sign and proximal muscle weakness — is paraneoplastic in adults, so it mandates a malignancy screen (see connective tissue disease). And always review the drug chart — a phototoxic drug is the commonest cause and is reversible on stopping it (see drug reactions).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Facial Rash:
On the face, distribution is diagnosis. Read which part of the face is involved and the morphology. Screen first for the emergencies: a sharply demarcated, hot, swollen red face with fever is erysipelas / cellulitis — and periorbital swelling with painful eye movements or proptosis is orbital cellulitis (see cellulitis); unilateral vesicles in the V1 dermatome with a lesion on the tip of the nose (Hutchinson’s sign) is herpes zoster ophthalmicus, a threat to sight (see viral infections). Then the inflammatory patterns: rosacea (central flushing, papulopustules, telangiectasia, no comedones) (see rosacea), acne (comedones) (see acne), seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy scale of the nasolabial folds / eyebrows) (see seborrhoeic dermatitis), and the autoimmune malar (butterfly) and heliotrope rashes (see malar rash, connective tissue disease). A photodistributed pattern points to photosensitivity.
🚨Some facial rashes threaten the eye or airway. Periorbital / orbital cellulitis — a swollen red eyelid with proptosis, painful or restricted eye movements, or reduced acuity — needs urgent imaging and IV antibiotics (see cellulitis). Herpes zoster ophthalmicus (V1 shingles with Hutchinson’s sign on the nose tip) can cause keratitis and sight loss → antivirals + ophthalmology (see viral infections). Erysipelas spreads fast (sharp, raised, red, febrile). And rapid lip / periorbital swelling (angioedema) can herald airway compromise (see urticaria / angioedema). Don’t forget the autoimmune faces — lupus and dermatomyositis (see connective tissue disease).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Nodosum:
Erythema nodosum is a reactive sign, not a disease — so recognising it is only step one; the real task is to find the trigger. The lesions are tender, red, raised subcutaneous nodules on the shins (the anterior lower legs), usually bilateral, that do not ulcerate and fade like bruises (a septal panniculitis / delayed hypersensitivity). The commonest cause is streptococcal infection (see streptococcal / tonsillitis); the ones you must not miss are tuberculosis (see tuberculosis), sarcoidosis — especially Löfgren’s syndrome (EN + bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy + arthralgia + fever, a good-prognosis presentation) (see sarcoidosis) — and inflammatory bowel disease (see IBD). Other triggers are drugs (sulfonamides, penicillins, the OCP) (see drug reactions), pregnancy, Behçet’s, and (in up to a third) idiopathic.
🚨Erythema nodosum is a window on systemic disease. Always investigate the cause: screen for tuberculosis (chest X-ray, IGRA) (see tuberculosis) and sarcoidosis — the combination of EN with bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy, arthralgia and fever is Löfgren’s syndrome (see sarcoidosis). Look for inflammatory bowel disease (diarrhoea, abdominal pain, weight loss) (see IBD), a preceding streptococcal throat infection (see streptococcal / tonsillitis), and, with oral / genital ulcers and uveitis, Behçet’s disease (see vasculitis). Review the drug chart and consider pregnancy. The nodules themselves are managed with rest, elevation and NSAIDs.

DERMATOLOGICAL__Pyoderma Gangrenosum:
Pyoderma gangrenosum is a neutrophilic ulcer that is easy to make worse. It starts as a pustule or nodule that rapidly breaks down into an enlarging, exquisitely painful ulcer with a characteristic violaceous, overhanging, undermined border. Two rules define its management. First, it shows pathergy — it is worsened by trauma, debridement and grafting, so do not debride it; it needs immunosuppression. Second, it is a diagnosis of exclusion — you must first rule out infection, vasculitis and malignancy with cultures and an edge biopsy (see skin infections, vasculitis). And it is a marker of systemic disease: hunt for inflammatory bowel disease (see IBD), rheumatoid / inflammatory arthritis (see rheumatoid arthritis) and haematological disease (myeloma, leukaemia, myelodysplasia) (see myeloma, leukaemia). For the wider ulcer differential, see the leg ulcers note.
🚨Do not debride pyoderma gangrenosum — and do not call it PG until you have excluded the mimics. Because of pathergy, surgical debridement or grafting can cause a dramatic, rapid enlargement of the ulcer; the treatment is immunosuppression (potent topical / systemic steroids, ciclosporin, or a TNF inhibitor). But PG is a clinical diagnosis of exclusion: a rapidly progressive ulcer can also be infection (including atypical / necrotising), vasculitis, or a malignancy — take an edge biopsy and cultures before committing (see skin infections, vasculitis). Once diagnosed, screen for IBD, rheumatoid arthritis and a haematological malignancy (see IBD, rheumatoid arthritis, myeloma).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Erythema Multiforme:
Erythema multiforme is defined by the target lesion. Look for “iris” (target) lesions — concentric rings with a dusky or blistered centre — distributed acrally on the extensor limbs, palms, soles and face. It is usually infection-triggered and self-limiting. The first question is minor or major? — EM minor has little or no mucosal involvement; EM major involves the mucosae (eyes, mouth, genitals). The commonest trigger is herpes simplex (recurrent EM) (see viral infections); in children, mycoplasma is important (mucosal-predominant, after a respiratory illness) (see pneumonia / mycoplasma); drugs are a less common cause (see drug reactions). The crucial distinction is from Stevens-Johnson syndrome / TEN — a drug-induced spectrum of widespread dusky macules with skin pain and detachment and a far worse prognosis (see dermatological emergencies, blistering rash).
🚨Separate erythema multiforme from SJS / TEN. EM has typical acral target lesions, is usually infection-triggered (HSV, mycoplasma) and carries a good prognosis. SJS / TEN is drug-induced, with widespread dusky / atypical macules, prominent skin pain, blistering and detachment (positive Nikolsky) and marked mucosal involvement — a medical emergency; stop the drug and treat like a burn (see dermatological emergencies). Within EM, major disease with ocular involvement needs ophthalmology to prevent scarring, and mucosal disease needs fluids and mouth / eye care. Recurrent EM is usually driven by HSV and may need suppressive antivirals (see viral infections).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Malar (Butterfly) Rash:
A malar (butterfly) rash is erythema across the cheeks and the bridge of the nose — and the single most useful sign is whether it spares the nasolabial folds. The acute cutaneous lupus of SLE is photosensitive, non-scarring and characteristically spares the nasolabial folds, and comes with systemic features (arthralgia, mouth ulcers, serositis, renal disease) (see connective tissue disease). Its main mimics favour the folds: seborrhoeic dermatitis (greasy scale) (see seborrhoeic dermatitis) and rosacea (central flushing, papulopustules, telangiectasia) (see rosacea). Don’t miss dermatomyositis (heliotrope + Gottron’s + weakness, paraneoplastic) (see connective tissue disease). In children, bright red “slapped cheeks” is parvovirus B19 (see childhood exanthems); a hot, tender, sharply demarcated cheek with fever is erysipelas (see cellulitis). Look for a photodistributed pattern (see photosensitive rash).
🚨A malar rash can be the face of systemic disease. A photosensitive butterfly rash sparing the nasolabial folds with arthralgia, mouth ulcers, hair loss, serositis or renal / haematological disease is systemic lupus erythematosus — check ANA, anti-dsDNA, complement and urinalysis (see connective tissue disease). A heliotrope rash with Gottron’s papules and proximal weakness is dermatomyositis — paraneoplastic in adults, so screen for malignancy (see connective tissue disease). And a sharply demarcated, hot, tender red cheek with fever is erysipelas / facial cellulitis, not lupus (see cellulitis).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Livedo Reticularis:
Livedo reticularis is a netlike, violaceous mottling of the skin from sluggish flow in the dermal vascular network. The first question is reversible or fixed? Physiological livedo (cutis marmorata) is a fine, complete, symmetrical net that reverses with warming — benign, common in infants and in the cold. Pathological livedo — especially livedo racemosa (larger, broken, irregular rings that persist on warming) — signals vessel occlusion or inflammation. The must-not-miss causes are antiphospholipid syndrome (livedo + arterial / venous thrombosis, stroke, miscarriage — Sneddon’s) (see connective tissue disease), cholesterol embolism (after an arterial procedure) (see renal vascular) and polyarteritis nodosa and other vasculitides (see vasculitis). Other causes include SLE, cryoglobulinaemia, DIC (see DIC), calciphylaxis, infection and drugs.
🚨Fixed, broken livedo (racemosa) is a warning of a thrombotic or vasculitic disease. Think antiphospholipid syndrome — livedo with stroke, DVT / PE, recurrent miscarriage or thrombocytopenia — and check antiphospholipid antibodies (see connective tissue disease). Cholesterol (atheroembolism) after angiography or vascular surgery causes livedo with blue toes, renal impairment and eosinophilia (see renal vascular). Polyarteritis nodosa gives livedo racemosa with nodules, mononeuritis multiplex, hypertension and renal disease (see vasculitis). And livedo with purpura, skin necrosis and coagulopathy suggests DIC (see DIC, purpuric rash).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Suspicious Skin Lesion (:
A “suspicious skin lesion” is a keratinocyte cancer until proven otherwise. The two common non-melanoma skin cancers have distinct faces. Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) is a pearly / translucent papule with telangiectasia, a rolled edge and central ulceration (a rodent ulcer) — slow-growing, locally destructive, rarely metastasising. Squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) is a keratotic, crusted, ulcerated, tender nodule that grows faster and can metastasise — especially on the lip or ear, in a scar (Marjolin’s), or in the immunosuppressed (see skin cancer). Know the pre-malignant lesions — actinic keratoses (rough, scaly, sun-damaged skin), Bowen’s disease (SCC in situ, a scaly plaque) and keratoacanthoma (a rapid dome with a keratin plug). And never forget melanoma — any changing, ulcerating or pigmented lesion (see pigmented lesion). A non-healing, bleeding or ulcerating lesion earns an urgent referral.
🚨Refer the lesion that will not heal. A new, growing, ulcerating or bleeding skin lesion in an adult — particularly a keratotic or tender nodule — needs an urgent (2-week-wait) referral and biopsy for squamous cell carcinoma, which has real metastatic potential when it is on the lip / ear, is large or poorly differentiated, arises in a scar, or occurs in an immunosuppressed (e.g. transplant) patient (see skin cancer). Always consider melanoma (including amelanotic forms) for any changing lesion (see pigmented lesion). Basal cell carcinoma rarely metastasises but is locally destructive and should still be excised. A subungual or acral lesion has its own pitfalls (see nail changes).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Cellulitis / Spreading E:
Hot, tender, spreading erythema is cellulitis until two questions are answered. First: is there a necrotising infection or sepsis? Pain out of proportion, rapid spread, crepitus, skin necrosis or haemorrhagic bullae and systemic toxicity mean necrotising fasciitis — a surgical emergency (see skin infections); tachycardia, hypotension and confusion mean sepsis → Sepsis 6 (see sepsis). Second: is it really cellulitis? True cellulitis is usually unilateral, hot, tender, poorly demarcated, spreading, with fever and a portal of entry (tinea, a wound, an ulcer) (see cellulitis); erysipelas is more superficial and sharply demarcated. Cellulitis is over-diagnosed — bilateral, chronic, itchy lower-leg redness is usually venous eczema (see chronic venous insufficiency), and other mimics include DVT (see DVT), acute gout (see crystal arthropathy) and erythema migrans (see Lyme disease).
🚨Necrotising fasciitis hides behind “cellulitis”. Suspect it when there is pain out of proportion to the skin signs, rapid spread, crepitus, dusky skin / haemorrhagic bullae / necrosis, or systemic toxicity — it is a surgical emergency needing urgent debridement and broad-spectrum antibiotics (see skin infections). Any spreading erythema with sepsis (tachycardia, hypotension, confusion) triggers the Sepsis 6 (see sepsis). On the face, periorbital / orbital cellulitis threatens the eye (see facial rash). And do not treat bilateral chronic venous eczema as infection — that is the commonest misdiagnosis (see chronic venous insufficiency).

DERMATOLOGICAL__Skin Lump / Nodule:
Describe a skin lump the way you would any lump — and decide benign or worrying. Assess site, size, shape, surface, consistency, mobility, tethering and overlying skin, and the history of growth. Most cutaneous lumps are benign: an epidermoid (sebaceous) cyst (a mobile lump with a central punctum), a lipoma (soft, mobile, lobulated, with a “slip sign”), a dermatofibroma (firm, dimples on pinching), skin tags, neurofibromas and reactive lymph nodes (see benign skin lumps). The red-flag lump is hard, fixed, deep, growing, >5 cm, tethered or ulcerating — think skin cancer (BCC / SCC / melanoma), soft-tissue sarcoma, a cutaneous metastasis (including a Sister Mary Joseph umbilical nodule) or lymphoma / leukaemia cutis (see skin cancer, suspicious skin lesion, pigmented lesion, lymphoma).
🚨Some lumps must be imaged and biopsied, not watched. A lump that is hard, fixed / tethered, deep to the fascia, larger than 5 cm, or growing is a soft-tissue sarcoma until an MRI and biopsy prove otherwise — refer urgently. A pearly, keratotic, ulcerating or changing lesion is a skin cancer (see suspicious skin lesion, pigmented lesion). Firm cutaneous nodules can be metastases — a Sister Mary Joseph nodule at the umbilicus signals an intra-abdominal malignancy — or lymphoma / leukaemia cutis (with B symptoms and lymphadenopathy) (see lymphoma, lymphadenopathy). Rapid growth, pain, fixation and systemic symptoms are the warnings.

DERMATOLOGICAL__Flushing:
Flushing is transient reddening of the skin — usually the face, neck and upper chest — from cutaneous vasodilation. Most is benign and physiological: emotion, heat, exercise, fever, hot drinks, spicy food and alcohol, the menopause (hot flushes) (see menopause), rosacea (see rosacea), and drugs (niacin, calcium-channel blockers, nitrates) (see drug reactions). But episodic flushing with the right company flags serious, treatable disease: carcinoid syndrome (flushing + diarrhoea + wheeze + right-heart valve disease), phaeochromocytoma (paroxysmal hypertension, headache, sweating, palpitations) (see phaeochromocytoma), systemic mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa, raised tryptase), medullary thyroid cancer (raised calcitonin, MEN2) (see thyroid cancer), and anaphylaxis (see anaphylaxis). Ask about triggers, associated symptoms and the pattern.
🚨Flushing with company is the clue to a secretory tumour. Carcinoid syndrome — flushing with diarrhoea, wheeze and right-sided heart murmurs — needs urinary 5-HIAA and chromogranin A. Phaeochromocytoma — paroxysmal hypertension with headache, sweating and palpitations — needs plasma / urinary metanephrines (see phaeochromocytoma); do not provoke it. Systemic mastocytosis (flushing, urticaria pigmentosa, anaphylaxis) needs a serum tryptase, and medullary thyroid carcinoma (flushing, diarrhoea, a neck lump, MEN2) a calcitonin (see thyroid cancer). And flushing with urticaria, wheeze or hypotension is anaphylaxis → IM adrenaline (see anaphylaxis).
